meldungen.titel: Washington tightens the screws on Nvidia as Jensen Huang's allies lobby for his return
meldungen.text:
Four days after Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive of Nvidia, the world's most valuable chipmaker is being pulled in two directions at once. On one side, the US Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, told Fox News on Sunday that the company needs a "dramatic shakeup" and should hire its next boss from outside. He gave the board and its outside counsel ten days to explain whether Nvidia ignored warning signs about shell companies, many of them in Singapore, that allegedly funnelled export-controlled AI chips to China, and whether any of this reached the C-suite. Were Nvidia a bank, he added, regulators would already be on site and many executives would be gone.

On the other side, the Financial Times reports that Huang has discussed a comeback with close allies, while Silicon Valley insiders and employees press the board to reinstate him. An open letter demanding that Nvidia "bring Jensen back" has gathered more than 150,000 signatures and won public backing from Elon Musk and Epic Games' Tim Sweeney, although its tally is hard to verify: Business Insider found entries such as "Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor". Even one of Huang's allies conceded to the FT that an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offence.

The background is lurid. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years at the helm, following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a senior colleague and one with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies suspect her of being a Chinese intelligence asset, and the Singapore company of smuggling some 2 billion dollars' worth of restricted chips into China. Megaspeed now says she left on 30 August 2025. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is running Nvidia on an interim basis; the company has opened an internal investigation with the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz and has reportedly approached Arm's chief executive, Rene Haas. AMD's Lisa Su is named as another plausible outsider, while Donald Trump has floated Tim Cook.

Congress, meanwhile, smells an opportunity. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Banking Committee chairman Tim Scott want Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, and House Speaker Mike Johnson speaks of a "growing consensus" on limiting chip exports to China. Bessent, by contrast, argues the rules already exist and merely need enforcing, and has accused Lutnick's department of dragging its feet on blacklisting Megaspeed.

The stakes are considerable: Nvidia shed roughly a trillion dollars of market value in a single week and has lost its most effective lobbyist in Washington. The next test comes quickly, with quarterly results due tomorrow, in a week when investors are also watching Anthropic's stock market debut and a DAX that has just closed a record week.

meldungen.titel: Cisco recruits Claude Mythos to attack corporate AI agents before criminals do
meldungen.text:
Cisco is folding Anthropic's Claude Mythos, the restricted model built for offensive security work, into its AI Defense platform. Announced at Cisco Live in the Asia Pacific region on 9 November, the integration lets security teams test whether their companies' AI agents can be manipulated into leaking data, misusing the tools they are connected to or taking actions nobody authorised. Mythos devises multi-step attacks tailored to each individual system, rather than firing a generic battery of prompts at it.

The guard rails are tight. Tests run only against systems that customers have registered and explicitly cleared; there is no open prompt access, and every test is logged against a named person. Mythos supplements Cisco's existing adaptive red-teaming engine rather than replacing it, and it will reach a select group of enterprises first, with no date yet for general availability. Cisco has not published an independent assessment of how well Mythos performs.

The move fits a broader pattern. Mythos launched in April as a preview for around fifty large organisations, among them Cisco, Google, Microsoft and the Linux Foundation, and IBM said last week it would bring the model to its own security customers. As companies hand agents real permissions, finding the weak spots before an attacker does has become a business in its own right. Testing alone fixes nothing, though: firms still need runtime protection, tightly scoped agent permissions and a process for closing the holes that red teams uncover.

meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 1: a map of the industry, from MBB to the Big Four and the boutiques
meldungen.text:
Before comparing exits, it helps to know the terrain. The first thing to grasp is that the familiar "tiers" are not official. No industry body assigns them; they are a recruiting convention, popularised largely by case-coaching websites with commercial interests of their own. The most objective inputs those sites cite are the Vault Consulting 50 and Forbes lists. Still, the convention matters, because recruiters, alumni networks and private equity funds think in exactly these categories.

At the top sit McKinsey, BCG and Bain, known collectively as MBB. In the 2026 Vault survey McKinsey ranks first for prestige in all three regions, and in North America Bain overtook BCG for second place for the first time on record. Size differs more than prestige. BCG, the only one of the three that publishes figures, reported revenue of 14.4 billion dollars for 2025, up 7 %, with 33,500 staff, and says AI and technology work now accounts for over 40 % of revenue. McKinsey no longer publishes numbers; its revenue is usually estimated at around 16 billion dollars, and Fortune reported a headcount decline of more than 10 % over roughly eighteen months. Forbes estimates Bain at about 7.5 billion dollars, with between 17,500 and 19,000 people depending on the source. One 2026 guide puts MBB acceptance rates at 1 to 3 %.

The second tier is usually given as Oliver Wyman, Roland Berger, L.E.K., Kearney and AlixPartners, with OC&C often grouped alongside. These firms are smaller and frequently stronger in particular niches (Oliver Wyman in financial services, Roland Berger in industry and restructuring, L.E.K. and OC&C in commercial due diligence), and, according to the same guide, hire 5 to 15 % of applicants with somewhat more humane hours. For a career in the German-speaking world, Roland Berger carries more weight than the global lists suggest, given its Munich roots.

Third come the strategy arms of the Big Four: Monitor Deloitte, Strategy& (PwC), EY-Parthenon and KPMG's strategy group. Formally they sit inside audit and advisory giants, but in practice EY-Parthenon and Strategy& behave much like tier-two firms, with close links to transaction services and deals. Beyond them lie specialist boutiques (Simon-Kucher for pricing, zeb for banks, Analysys Mason for telecoms and media) and the in-house consultancies of large corporations.

In Germany the market is large and still growing: Lünendonk puts management consulting at 51.1 billion euros, the first time it has passed the 50-billion mark, with the German top 20 growing 4.1 % and the international firms 3.0 %. Porsche Consulting ranks fifth among German-owned firms. Lünendonk does not rank the global players by German revenue, so claims about who is "biggest in Germany" deserve some scepticism.

The coming parts of this series take each firm in turn, starting with McKinsey's practices, its entry routes and where its alumni end up.

meldungen.titel: McKinsey makes the case that AI agents can pay for themselves within a year at banks
meldungen.text:
McKinsey's latest Global Banking Annual Review, subtitled "The AI disruption dividend", is doing the rounds this morning, with Indian media headlining that AI agents could help banks generate nearly three times their returns over three years. The report itself, as far as it can be checked, is more granular. It examines payback periods and three-year returns on investment across 52 use cases and concludes that purpose-built agentic AI typically recoups its cost in around ten months. One bank example in the report expected a set of customer-support agents to return roughly 2.8 times the initial investment within a single year.

The message continues a line McKinsey has pushed for some time: the gains from AI in banking accrue to institutions that rebuild whole processes around agents rather than bolting chatbots onto old ones, and laggards risk seeing profits eroded. The headline three-year multiple could not be verified in the published text, so treat it as the media's gloss rather than McKinsey's own figure.

meldungen.titel: Vanguard extends shareholder voting choice to its FTSE All-World ETF, but not yet to private savers
meldungen.text:
Vanguard is bringing its Investor Choice programme, which lets fund holders pick the proxy voting policy applied to their share of a fund, to Europe. From 2027 four Ireland-domiciled funds and ETFs join, among them the Vanguard FTSE All-World UCITS ETF, one of the most widely held building blocks in European savings plans. With the additions, eight funds holding roughly 200 billion pounds in total are covered, according to Portfolio Adviser.

The mechanics are straightforward: eligible investors choose from a menu of voting policies, and Vanguard casts the votes attached to their holdings accordingly. According to Vanguard's notice to investors in its Irish funds, sign-ups open today, 16 November, and the programme runs from around 1 March to 30 June 2027, covering the main season of annual general meetings.

There is a catch for private savers. In Europe the scheme is open only to professional intermediaries that meet eligibility criteria, not to individuals, unlike the US version, which has grown to more than half a million participants and 151 billion dollars of assets. The broader point is political: index giants hold such large stakes that how they vote on boards, pay and climate resolutions has become contentious, and passing the choice down the chain is their answer. Trade press reporting suggests the US programme has so far changed voting outcomes very little.

meldungen.titel: Security trumps salary: German students' job priorities flip as confidence slumps
meldungen.text:
For the first time in EY's regular student survey, job security has overtaken pay as the most important criterion in choosing an employer. Of more than 2,000 students polled online in spring 2026, 52 % named a secure position, ten percentage points more than two years earlier, when salary and the prospect of raises had led the field. Pay has now slipped to second place.

The shift tracks the economy. Only 39 % of respondents said they were confident of finding a suitable job quickly after graduating, a fall of fifteen points since 2024, as Germany's industrial slump filters through to graduate hiring. EY describes the survey as representative.

The consultancy's own advice is that graduates should not chase safety alone, lest they miss opportunities. It is a familiar tension: in downturns, large and stable employers attract a surge of applications, while smaller firms and fast-growing sectors can be easier to get into and offer steeper learning curves. The findings, first published by dpa in late October, are being picked up again this week by regional papers.

meldungen.titel: Why you struggle out of bed in November: your biological night really is longer
meldungen.text:
Swiss broadcaster SRF leads its science coverage this morning with winter sleep, under the headline that people sleep about twenty minutes longer in winter. The mechanism is one the sleep researcher Christine Blume has explained on SRF before: our internal biological night lasts somewhat longer in the dark months than in summer, so many people need a little more sleep and oversleep more easily.

Precise numbers are slippery. A frequently cited 2023 sleep-lab analysis of around 188 people found participants slept roughly an hour longer in winter than in summer, but the difference in total sleep was not statistically significant and the sample was not representative; the more robust finding was an increase in REM sleep. Popular health outlets cite studies suggesting fifteen to twenty minutes more sleep when temperatures drop, and some doctors advise budgeting an extra twenty to thirty minutes in winter.

The practical upshot is modest but useful: if you feel sluggish now, it is probably biology rather than a lack of discipline. Going to bed a little earlier, getting daylight in the morning and keeping wake-up times consistent are the standard recommendations.

meldungen.titel: Volkswagen bets on a smaller, leaner group: nine million cars and fatter margins by 2030
meldungen.text:
Volkswagen's chief executive Oliver Blume has restated the group's ambitions for 2030, as WirtschaftsWoche and others report this weekend: around nine million vehicles a year and markedly higher profitability. The volume target is less bold than it sounds. Last year all group brands together delivered 8.98 million vehicles, so the plan is essentially to hold sales flat while shrinking the machine behind them.

That is the strategic core of the "Zukunftsplan 2030" approved by the supervisory board. Production capacity is to fall from more than twelve million vehicles to about nine million, the number of models is to be roughly halved, and 50,000 jobs are to go across the group by 2030, a reduction Blume says is on schedule; 28,000 of those cuts are already settled. The financial target is an operating return on sales of 9 % by 2030, worth around 31 billion euros of operating profit, although Blume has also spoken of a range of 8 to 10 %. The group's operating margin currently stands at 3.8 %.

It is a textbook choice of profitability over volume: after years of chasing scale, Wolfsburg aims to match capacity to demand, cut complexity and lift margins, with defence work also on the table as a new line of business. Blume says capital markets are beginning to reward the progress. Whether a company of VW's size can more than double its margin while Chinese competitors press into Europe is the question analysts will keep asking.
